messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 50
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Plumber
- Trauma Type: Assault
- Pcl5: 73

He is a 50-year-old African man who has spent most of his adult life working with his hands. As a plumber, he is used to entering other people’s homes quietly, noticing what is leaking, what is blocked, what needs pressure or release. Before the assault, he describes himself as steady and practical, the one in his family who kept things running. He is married, and for years his life has followed a dependable rhythm: early mornings, a thermos of tea in the van, long days moving between apartment blocks and private houses, then home in the evening to his wife.

The assault happens on an ordinary workday. He is called to fix a burst pipe in a neighborhood he does not know well. By the time he finishes, it is getting dark. As he loads his tools back into the van, two men approach him. At first he thinks they want directions or help. Instead, they demand his money and phone. He hesitates, confused more than defiant, and one of them strikes him hard across the face. He falls against the side of the van. He remembers the metallic smell of his tools, the cold pavement under one hand, and the strange, sharp thought that he might be killed over a bag of wrenches. They kick him while he tries to protect his head. He hears one man shouting, though later he cannot remember the words. What stays with him is the helplessness: his body curled in on itself, his chest locked, his voice gone. When they leave, taking his wallet and phone, he remains on the ground for several minutes, unable to trust that it is over.

In the weeks afterward, he tells people he is “lucky.” He goes back to work quickly because he feels he has no choice. But the world has changed shape. He cannot stand the sound of footsteps behind him. When he parks the van, he checks mirrors repeatedly before getting out. If a stranger walks too close while he is unloading equipment, his heart starts pounding so hard he feels it in his neck. He startles at sudden movement and becomes ashamed of it immediately. He is a large, capable man, someone who has spent years solving practical problems, and he cannot understand why his body now reacts as if danger is everywhere.

Sleep becomes one of the first things he loses. He lies down exhausted but cannot settle. Just as he drifts off, he is back beside the van, bracing for the next blow. Sometimes he dreams it in fragments: a shoe coming toward his ribs, breath knocked out of him, his own hands failing to protect him. He wakes sweating, already tense, and walks through the house checking locks. His wife asks what is wrong, but he struggles to explain it without feeling humiliated. He becomes quieter with her, less patient, easily irritated by small things—the television volume, a misplaced key, a question asked at the wrong moment. He sees the hurt in her face and hates himself for bringing this hardness into their home.

At work, he starts turning down evening callouts and jobs in unfamiliar areas. He tells clients he is fully booked. He takes longer routes to avoid the street where the assault happened, then begins avoiding whole sections of the city. When he does enter apartment buildings, he scans stairwells and listens for voices in corridors instead of focusing on the pipes. He keeps his tools closer than necessary, not because he plans to use them, but because being empty-handed feels intolerable. Sometimes a customer will approach him unexpectedly from behind while he is crouched under a sink, and he jerks up so suddenly that he bangs his head or drops what he is holding. He laughs it off, but afterward his hands shake too much to work cleanly.

He also carries a heavier, more private burden: the sense that something essential in him has been damaged. He replays the assault and searches for the moment he should have fought harder, run sooner, seen it coming. He knows, when he speaks calmly, that he was overpowered. But in unguarded moments he thinks of himself as weak, exposed, no longer the protector he believed himself to be. He sits in his van between jobs staring at the steering wheel, unable to force himself to start the engine. Crowded petrol stations, young men gathering on corners, even laughter behind him can flood him with dread before his mind has caught up.

His wife notices that he no longer lingers outside in the evening or visits friends as he used to. He prefers the safety of home, but even there he is not fully at rest. He sits where he can see the door. He listens for sounds at night. He says he is tired all the time, yet rest never seems to reach him. Months later, he is still living as though the assault is not in the past but just about to happen again.
